query: For high-entropy-alloy bond coats used in thermal barrier coating systems for high-temperature applications, what single intervention could improve coating durability and reliability? Formulate one hypothesis specifying the intervention, its mechanism, the predicted improvement relative to an untreated baseline, the conditions under which it should remain effective, prior evidence supporting it, and an experiment with a clear result that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Introducing a small amount of zirconium into a high‐entropy alloy bond coat will promote in‐situ formation of a graded interfacial layer (e.g., a Hf–Zr mixed phase) that enhances adhesion between the bond coat and the substrate, thereby reducing oxide scale spallation and improving durability under high-temperature thermal cycling in TBC systems.
generation.material_initial_state: A conventional high-entropy alloy bond coat (e.g., an AlCoCrFeNi-based system, or similar composition without Zr) that, under high-temperature operation, is prone to interfacial delamination and nonuniform thermally grown oxide formation.
generation.intervention: Incorporate a low concentration (on the order of 1–2 at%) of zirconium into the high-entropy alloy formulation prior to deposition, using a process such as laser cladding or hot-press sintering.
generation.conditions: High-temperature environmental conditions typical of TBC applications, e.g., thermal cycling between ambient and approximately 900–1100 °C in oxidizing or salt-contaminated atmospheres.
generation.structural_mediator: The formation of a gradient intermetallic or mixed oxide layer (such as a Hf–Zr enriched zone) at the bond coat/substrate interface.
generation.mechanism: Zirconium, as a reactive element with favorable diffusivity at high temperatures, will migrate toward the interface during service. There it forms a graded transition layer with existing elements (such as Hf) that reduces thermal expansion mismatch and improves metallurgical bonding. The improved interfacial structure promotes the formation of a uniform and adherent thermally grown oxide (e.g., an α-Al2O3 scale) that minimizes spallation during thermal cycling.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to undoped bond coats, the Zr-doped coating should exhibit a noticeably lower area of oxide scale spallation, reduced incidence of interfacial delamination, and overall improved durability and reliability during long-term high-temperature exposure and thermal cycling.
generation.baseline: Performance metrics (e.g., TGO spallation area, interfacial adhesion strength, oxidation degradation rate) of high-entropy alloy bond coats without zirconium doping under similar high-temperature and cyclic oxidation conditions.
generation.boundary: The beneficial effect is expected only for low-level Zr additions; doping levels significantly higher than ~2 at% may form excessive brittle phases that could compromise mechanical performance. Additionally, the effect may depend on the specific base alloy composition and processing route used to fabricate the bond coat.
generation.uncertainty: The hypothesis builds on evidence from the VZrHfNbTa high-entropy alloy coating work (PMC10488483, where Zr diffusion improved bonding and reduced peeling) and from studies on reactive-element additions (e.g., Y and Hf co-doping improving oxidation behavior in AlCoCrFeNi-based coatings as discussed in PMC10488378). What is new is extending the concept specifically to bond coats in TBC systems, focusing on interfacial durability and reliability under cyclic thermal loads. Uncertainty remains regarding the optimal Zr concentration and how exactly the graded interfacial phase develops under service conditions.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of high-entropy alloy bond coats on identical substrate materials using an identical deposition process. One set is fabricated with a standard formulation (no Zr) and the other with a targeted low-level Zr doping (1–2 at%). Subject both sets to accelerated thermal cycling and high-temperature oxidation tests in a corrosive environment (e.g., with Na2SO4/NaCl deposits) over an extended period.
measurements: Quantitative assessment of TGO spallation area (via image analysis of cross-sections after testing)
Interfacial adhesion strength (using pull-off or shear tests)
Microstructural analysis (via SEM/EDS) to identify graded interfacial layer formation and oxide scale uniformity
Oxidation weight gain and mechanical property retention over cycles
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the Zr-doped bond coats do not show a statistically significant improvement in adhesion strength and a reduction in oxide spallation area compared to undoped samples, or if they exhibit deleterious brittle phases that impair mechanical integrity, the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: In this work, AlCoCrFeNi2.1 EHEA and co-doping Y and Hf AlCoCrFeNi2.1 YHf-EHEA coatings were successfully prepared by laser cladding. The solidification microstructure, thermal stability, and hot corrosion of the coatings at 900 °C under 75% Na2SO4 + 25% NaCl molten salts were investigated. 1. The YHf co-doping did not alter the solidification microstructure and phase structure of the EHEA coating. The microstructure morphologies of the top and bottom portions of coatings were composed of cellular and columnar dendrites, respectively. And the phase structure consisted of FCC and BCC/B2. 2. After heat treatment at 900 °C for 10 h, the BCC/B2 structure was relatively stable in all coatings while the nanoscale Al-rich L12 phase was precipitated in the FCC. 3. The grain sizes of the HT-EHEA and HT-YHf coatings after heat treatment at 900 °C for 10 h increased by 27.5% and 15.7%, respectively, compared to the as-deposited coatings. Additionally, the volume fractions of the LAGBs decreased by 13.9% and 8.3% in the HT-EHEA and HT-YHf coatings, respectively. 4.
